analysis.one_liner: Restructures health insurance around tax-advantaged savings accounts, market competition, and looser insurance rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it was referred to nine House committees in July 2022 and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Care Act of 2022 is a broad Republican alternative to the Affordable Care Act. It would expand health savings accounts so they can be paired with almost any health plan, repeal the employer coverage mandate, create new tax credits for people who buy coverage, and let insurers charge older adults up to five times what younger adults pay (current law allows three times). It also adds price transparency rules, antitrust action against hospital consolidation, faster generic drug approvals, limits on pharmacy benefit managers, expanded telehealth coverage, a monthly cap on Medicare drug costs, and federal limits on medical malpractice lawsuits. The bill was sent to nine committees and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income investors gain from repealing the 3.8% net investment income tax. Savers who can fund health savings accounts gain a more flexible, tax-sheltered vehicle usable with nearly any plan, including bankruptcy protection. Younger and healthier enrollees would likely see lower premiums as rating rules loosen. Self-employed people and small businesses gain from new credits and freedom from the employer mandate. Patients gain telehealth expansion, a monthly Medicare drug cost cap, hospital price transparency, and curbs on anticompetitive hospital contracts and pharmacy benefit manager practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, HSA users, and younger enrollees

how_it_helps.text: Health savings accounts could be paired with nearly any health plan — employer plans, individual plans, Medicare, Medicaid, VA, TRICARE, and health care sharing ministries — instead of only high-deductible plans, with annual contribution limits of $3,600 to $5,000 depending on plan generosity and a $50,000 account cap.

The bill maintains guaranteed availability of coverage in the individual and group market and prohibits insurers from setting eligibility rules based on health status, medical condition, claims experience, genetic information, or disability.
It adds a new low-premium 'copper' plan tier to the exchanges and creates refundable tax credits for qualified health plans for people offered employer coverage.

It imposes price transparency requirements on hospitals and insurers, requires plan oversight of pharmacy benefit managers, eliminates DIR fees that PBMs charge pharmacies, and bans anticompetitive contract terms that limit patient access to higher quality, lower cost care.

It gives the Federal Trade Commission authority over certain tax-exempt hospitals and addresses hospital consolidation, and speeds up development and approval of generic complex drugs and biosimilars.

It caps Medicare prescription drug cost-sharing on a monthly basis and requires manufacturer rebates for Part B drugs whose prices rise faster than inflation, and it greatly expands coverage of telehealth services, including mental health telehealth and its use by rural clinics and Native American health facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Older adults would pay more for insurance, since premiums could rise to five times the young-adult rate instead of three. People with significant health needs could face less stable risk pools if short-term limited duration plans and looser plan rules draw healthier customers out. Workers with generous employer coverage would lose some current tax exclusions, making that coverage partly taxable. Injured patients would face federal limits on malpractice claims, including restrictions on expert testimony and requirements for affidavits of merit. High-income households benefit from a tax cut while the bill's own new credits and programs need offsetting revenue from those same coverage tax exclusions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Older and sicker enrollees, and injured patients

drawbacks.text: The bill would allow adult premiums to vary by age up to 5 to 1, compared with the 3 to 1 limit in current law, shifting a larger share of premium costs onto people in their 50s and 60s.

It would repeal the net investment income tax, a 3.8% tax on investment income that falls mainly on high-income households, cutting their taxes while the bill raises new revenue by making some employer-provided coverage taxable to ordinary workers.

It would expand short-term limited duration insurance plans, which are cheaper but do not have to cover preexisting conditions or comprehensive benefits, and which can siphon healthier people out of the regulated market and raise costs for those who remain.

Its medical malpractice title would restrict expert witness testimony, require an affidavit of merit before filing, and change how future damages are paid, which supporters say deters frivolous suits but which could reduce compensation for patients genuinely harmed by malpractice.

Employer health savings account contributions would be tied to specific plan rules and class-based contribution formulas, and the bill terminates several existing tax-favored arrangements — FSAs, Archer MSAs, and most HRAs — forcing households to move into the new HSA structure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine attempt at comprehensive reform with real consumer wins: telehealth expansion, a Medicare drug cost cap, hospital price transparency, antitrust action against consolidation, and PBM curbs all would have helped patients. But its centerpiece is shifting health financing into tax-advantaged savings accounts, which work best for people with spare income to save and offer little to households living paycheck to paycheck, and it loosens rating rules in ways that raise costs for older and sicker enrollees while cutting taxes for high-income investors. It was also never scored, never debated, and never amended, so its many interacting provisions — from Medicare premium restructuring to the repeal of several tax exclusions — were never examined in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 28, 2022, referred to nine House committees, and a few of its provisions were sent to Judiciary subcommittees in November; no committee ever marked it up and no chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bruce Westerman introduced the Fair Care Act of 2022 on July 28, 2022, joined by Representative Gonzalez of Ohio.
The bill was referred to nine committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and Labor, Judiciary, Oversight and Reform, Rules, Budget, Armed Services, and House Administration.
In November 2022, three Judiciary subcommittees received referrals of the provisions within their jurisdiction; no further action of any kind was recorded.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill still sitting in committee; it was never reported out, never scheduled for a floor vote, and never considered in the Senate.
The bill's one cosponsor joined at introduction, and no other members signed on in the months that followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, existing law stayed exactly as it was: private insurers, hospitals, drug manufacturers, and pharmacy benefit managers kept operating under current rules, and no one — patient or industry — got the changes the bill proposed.

against.what_they_did: The committee of first referral never held a markup or hearing on the bill; the record shows no committee action beyond initial referral and subcommittee routing.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican-only bill: one sponsor and one cosponsor, both Republicans, in a Democratic-controlled House; no Democrat cosponsored it and the Democratic majority took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill keeps private insurance as the channel for coverage and routes new tax credits through qualified health plans, while repealing the employer mandate, expanding short-term plans, and loosening rating rules in insurers' favor. It does impose price transparency and network competition rules on them. [S3]

The bill targets hospital consolidation, extends FTC authority to tax-exempt hospitals, bans anticompetitive contract terms, requires price transparency, and moves Medicare to site-neutral payment for off-campus departments — all aimed at hospital pricing power that drives up patient costs.
The bill requires plan oversight of PBM services, increases transparency of PBM pricing, and eliminates DIR fees that PBMs charge pharmacies, reducing a revenue stream largely invisible to patients.

Faster generic and biosimilar pathways, consolidated exclusivity periods, and an inflation rebate for Part B drugs would cut into brand-drug pricing power, while provisional approvals and priority review channels offer them new commercial routes.

Repealing the net investment income tax eliminates a 3.8% tax on investment income borne by high earners, a direct tax cut funded in part by making some employer health coverage taxable to ordinary workers.

The employer mandate is repealed, but new corporations would be barred from claiming tax benefits for offering traditional insurance and would have to use HSA contributions, and several employee health account tax exclusions are terminated.

The malpractice title imposes federal procedural limits — affidavits of merit, expert witness qualification rules, structured payment of future damages — that reduce recoveries and the viability of claims for patients injured by malpractice.
